newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialist chief slams bugging secrecy.
newsitem.headline: French Socialist chief slams bugging secrecy.

text.p: French Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin has asked the government to lift "monarchical" secrecy shrouding widespread illegal wire-tapping under the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand.

Jospin said it was a breach of democracy to use official secrecy to obstruct a probe into evidence that Mitterrand's anti-terrorist unit spied on dozens of politicians, lawyers and journalists without judicial permission.

"I demand that Prime Minister Alain Juppe lift official secrecy. We have to do away with this monarchical secrecy, whoever the president involved is," Jospin told M6 television in an interview on Sunday night.
The issue is dividing Juppe's centre-right coalition.

Ex-defence minister Francois Leotard, whose own former aides were subjected to wiretaps by his successor, called for secrecy to be lifted. But former interior minister Charles Pasqua said it was needed to protect the state in highly sensitive cases.
Juppe has rejected a request by a former senior presidential aide to waive secrecy to allow him to prepare his defence.
The prime minister's office said the decision was in line with long-standing jurisprudence upheld by civil courts and the Council of State, France's highest administrative court.

Gilles Menage, who headed Mitterrand's private office in the early 1980s, had formally requested the waiver so that he could defend himself against charges of invasion of privacy "in equitable conditions".
Secret files from the now-disbanded anti-terrorist unit, published by the media last week, showed Mitterrand personally ordered telephone-tapping to protect his private life.

"If it's true, it's a sad story...It does not fit the idea I had of him," said Jospin, a political associate of Mitterrand who lost the 1995 presidential election to succeed him to Gaullist Jacques Chirac.
Menage has contended that all the wiretaps were justified on national security grounds.

Former Socialist minister Michel Charasse, a confidant of Mitterrand, said in a radio interview on Sunday the wire-tapping was necessary to protect the late president and his family because of "terrorist attacks" in 1982-86.
Killers had threatened to kidnap Mitterrand's illegitimate daughter Mazarine, whose existence was only made public in 1994, he said.
He also said the late writer Jean-Edern Hallier, a major target of the telephone-tapping, had demanded money in exchange for not revealing that Mitterrand had a child out of wedlock.
Relatives and associates of Hallier challenged Charasse to produce evidence to back his charges.
The daily Le Monde and the weekly L'Express published what they said were extracts from files seized by counter-espionage officers and investigating magistrates in February.

The archives, stored in a garage outside Paris rented by the unit's former head, Christian Prouteau, included recordings of telephone-taps, demands for presidential favours and memos on terrorism suspects.
Both reports said many notes destined for Mitterrand carried his laconic handwritten comment: "Vu" (Seen).
Prouteau, Menage, two former senior government officials and three members of the unit are being probed over the bugging.
